passages.happening:
After the battle, the LORD speaks to Abram in a vision: “Do not be afraid, Abram. I am your shield, your very great reward” (verse 1).

Abram answers honestly. He still has no child. His heir will be “Eliezer of Damascus”, a servant in his house (verses 2-3).

God says no: “one who comes from your own body will be your heir” (verse 4). He takes Abram outside and says, “Now look to the heavens and count the stars, if you are able.” Then he says, “So shall your offspring be” (verse 5).

Then comes one of the most important sentences in the Bible: “Abram believed the LORD, and it was credited to him as righteousness” (verse 6).
passages.hearers:
‘Shield’ was a word used for a king who protects his people. Abram has just fought a war and turned down Sodom's riches (14:22-23). God answers both: I will protect you, and I am your reward. (The Hebrew can also be read ‘your reward will be very great’, and some Bibles put it that way.)

Abram's question is real. A man with no son needed an heir, someone to inherit his household and carry on his name. If there was no son, a trusted servant might become the heir. That is what Abram expects.

God answers with the night sky. Away from city lights, the sky over the desert is crowded with stars. Abram cannot count them. And God says: your family will be like that.

Verse 6 has two hard words. ‘Believed’ means more than agreeing that something is true. It means trusting someone, leaning your weight on them. ‘Credited’ is a word for counting or reckoning, as a person counts something to someone's account. ‘Righteousness’ means being right with God. Abram has done nothing new. He has no child yet. He simply trusts God's word, and God counts that trust as righteousness.
passages.later:
Paul builds a whole argument on verse 6. He quotes it: “Abraham believed God, and it was credited to him as righteousness” (Romans 4:3; Galatians 3:6). He points out when it happened: “Was it after his circumcision, or before? It was not after, but before” (Romans 4:10). So Abraham is “the father of all who believe” (Romans 4:11), Jews and Gentiles alike.

Paul says Abraham faced the facts about his old body and Sarah's, “Yet he did not waver through disbelief in the promise of God” (Romans 4:20).

James quotes the same verse, and says it “was fulfilled” when Abraham offered Isaac years later (James 2:21-23). For James, faith that is real shows itself in what a person does: “his faith was working with his actions” (James 2:22).

Hebrews remembers the stars: from one man “as good as dead, came descendants as numerous as the stars in the sky” (Hebrews 11:12).
passages.hard:
How do Paul and James fit together, and what does ‘credited’ mean? Christians have argued about this for five hundred years, and both sides should be heard in their own words.

Paul says a person is counted right with God through faith, not by works of the law (Romans 4:5). James says “a man is justified by his deeds and not by faith alone” (James 2:24). To be justified means to be counted or made right with God. Many readers, Catholic and Protestant alike, say the two are not at war. Paul speaks of how Abraham was first counted right with God, in Genesis 15. James speaks of how that faith was shown to be real, in Genesis 22. Paul fights against trying to earn God's favor. James fights against a faith that never does anything.

The deeper difference is about ‘credited’. Protestant teachers, following Luther and Calvin, read it as God counting a person righteous by a righteousness that is not their own. On this reading, Christ's righteousness is put to the believer's account, as a gift. Catholic teaching, set out at the Council of Trent in 1547, holds that when God counts a person righteous he also truly makes them righteous, so that being counted right and being made new belong together. Catholic writers point out that ‘credited’ in Romans 4 does not rule out God's real work inside a person. Protestants answer that the renewal is real but is not the ground of being right with God.

These notes do not settle it. Both agree on what verse 6 puts first: God's promise, and Abram's trust in it, before anything Abram did.
passages.asks: Abram brought God his honest worry: I still have no child. God did not scold him. He took him outside to see the stars. Ask what worry you have not said to God out loud. Then ask what it would mean to lean your weight on what God has said, before you can see it.

passages.happening:
God speaks again: “I am the LORD, who brought you out of Ur of the Chaldeans to give you this land to possess” (verse 7).

Abram asks, “Lord GOD, how can I know that I will possess it?” (verse 8).

God tells him to bring “a heifer, a goat, and a ram, each three years old, along with a turtledove and a young pigeon” (verse 9). A heifer is a young cow. Abram cuts each large animal in two and lays the halves opposite each other, leaving a path between them. He does not cut the birds (verse 10).

Birds of prey come down on the bodies, and Abram drives them away (verse 11).
passages.hearers:
Abram has just believed God (verse 6), and now he asks for a sign. The two go together. Trusting God and asking him honest questions are not opposites.

God's answer would have made sense to an ancient reader. People made binding agreements this way. In Hebrew you ‘cut’ a covenant. A covenant is a binding promise that makes a lasting bond. The animals were cut in half, the halves laid in two rows, and the one making the promise walked between them.

The meaning was a curse on yourself: ‘May what happened to these animals happen to me if I break my word.’ An Aramaic treaty from Sefire in Syria, from the 700s BC, has a curse like this. It says, in effect, that as a calf is cut in two, so the king who breaks the treaty and his nobles will be cut in two.

The animals Abram brings are all animals that Israel's law later accepts for sacrifice. The birds of prey are a dark touch. Abram has to guard the covenant pieces while he waits.
passages.later:
The prophet Jeremiah describes this very custom. In his day the leaders of Judah made a covenant by cutting a calf in two and walking between the pieces, and then broke it. God says, “I will treat like the calf they cut in two in order to pass between its pieces” (Jeremiah 34:18). That is how we know what the ritual meant.

God's question to Abram, ‘How can I know?’, is answered in many places with signs. Gideon asks for a sign with a fleece (Judges 6:36-40), and God gives it. Thomas asks to see the wounds, and Jesus shows him (John 20:27).
passages.asks: Abram believed, and still asked, ‘How can I know?’ Ask whether you think questions are a lack of faith. Then bring your question to God the way Abram did, honestly and to his face.

passages.t: Four hundred years, and the Amorites
passages.happening:
As the sun sets, Abram falls into a deep sleep, “and suddenly great terror and darkness overwhelmed him” (verse 12).

God tells him what is coming. “Know for certain that your descendants will be strangers in a land that is not their own, and they will be enslaved and mistreated four hundred years” (verse 13). But God will judge that nation, and they will leave “with many possessions” (verse 14).

Abram himself will die in peace at a good old age (verse 15). “In the fourth generation your descendants will return here, for the iniquity of the Amorites is not yet complete” (verse 16).
passages.hearers:
The promise comes with bad news. Before the family receives the land, it will be enslaved in a foreign country. The first hearers knew who that country was: Egypt. This is the exodus story told in advance.

The numbers are given in more than one way. Here it is four hundred years and ‘the fourth generation’. Exodus says the stay in Egypt lasted 430 years (Exodus 12:40). Many readers take four hundred as a round number. The word for ‘generation’ can also mean a long lifetime. Ancient readers already counted these years in different ways.

The Amorites were one of the peoples of Canaan. Here the name stands for the people of the land as a whole. ‘Iniquity’ means wrongdoing. God says the time for judging them has not yet come. He will wait.
passages.later:
Exodus tells how it happened: “At the end of the 430 years, to the very day, all the LORD’s divisions went out of the land of Egypt” (Exodus 12:41). Paul counts from the promise to the law and says “The law that came 430 years later does not revoke the covenant previously established by God” (Galatians 3:17).

Deuteronomy says the land was not a reward for Israel's goodness: “It is not because of your righteousness or uprightness of heart that you are going in to possess their land, but it is because of their wickedness” (Deuteronomy 9:5). And Leviticus warns Israel that the same land will throw out Israel too if it does the same things (Leviticus 18:24-28). The exile later shows that this was not an empty threat.

Peter says, “The Lord is not slow in keeping His promise as some understand slowness, but is patient with you, not wanting anyone to perish” (2 Peter 3:9).
passages.hard:
Verse 16 looks ahead to Israel's later wars in Canaan, which Deuteronomy and Joshua describe in terms of total destruction. Many readers find those chapters some of the hardest in the Bible, and they are right to feel the weight.

This verse does not answer every question, but it says some things that matter. The judgment is described as late. Long before, God told Abraham his descendants would wait, “for the iniquity of the Amorites is not yet complete” (Genesis 15:16). On the Bible's own account, the peoples of Canaan were given generations. God waits four hundred years. The later war is described as judgment on long wrongdoing, not as one people being better than another. Israel is held to the same standard. And the line is not drawn by blood: Rahab of Jericho joins Israel, and “she has lived among the Israelites to this day” (Joshua 6:25).

The Honest Answer ‘Did God command genocide in the Old Testament?’ on this site faces the whole question at length. These notes say nothing against any people, ancient or modern. The Amorites are not a name for anyone living today.
passages.asks: God told Abram the hard part of the future, not only the good part. Ask whether you want a God who only promises good things, or one who tells you the truth. Then ask what it means that God was patient for four hundred years, with people who did not know him.

passages.t: The fire passes between the pieces
passages.happening:
“When the sun had set and darkness had fallen, behold, a smoking firepot and a flaming torch appeared and passed between the halves of the carcasses” (verse 17).

“On that day the LORD made a covenant with Abram” (verse 18). He names the land: from “the river of Egypt” to the River Euphrates (verse 18), the land of the Kenites, the Amorites, the Canaanites and other peoples (verses 19-21).
passages.hearers:
Here is the surprise. In this kind of ceremony, the one who made the promise walked between the pieces and called the curse down on himself.

But Abram does not walk at all. He is asleep. Only the firepot and the torch pass through. Fire and smoke are signs of God's presence all through the Old Testament: the burning bush, the pillar of fire, the smoke on Mount Sinai. So God alone passes between the pieces. He takes the whole weight of the promise on himself. It is as if God says: ‘May I be torn apart if I do not keep my word.’

The borders are very wide. Israel came near them only in the days of David and Solomon (1 Kings 4:21). The list of peoples reminds the reader again that the land was full of people already.
passages.later:
The fire that passes through the pieces is the fire God later shows Moses in a bush “ablaze with fire, but it was not consumed” (Exodus 3:2), and the “pillar of fire” that leads Israel out of Egypt (Exodus 13:21).

Hebrews says that when God made his promise to Abraham, “since He had no one greater to swear by, He swore by Himself” (Hebrews 6:13). It is “impossible for God to lie” (Hebrews 6:18).

Many Christians see in this scene a picture of the cross. Paul says, “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us” (Galatians 3:13). God took the curse of the broken covenant on himself. The New Testament does not draw this link from Genesis 15 directly. It is a Christian reading of the pattern, and it is offered as that.

On the land itself, Christians read the promise in more than one way. The note on Genesis 12:4-9 sets out the views. These notes take no side, and they make no claim about any modern state, border or conflict.
passages.asks: Abram slept while God bound himself with an oath. The promise did not depend on Abram's strength. Ask where you are trying to hold up your side of things with God by effort. Then ask what it would mean to rest in a promise God has kept by himself.
